lesson.title: Turning Light's Leftovers Into Sugar: The Calvin Cycle
lesson.summary: The Calvin cycle uses the ATP and NADPH generated by the light-dependent reactions to convert atmospheric carbon dioxide into the three-carbon sugar building blocks that plants use to construct glucose.
lesson.body:
The light-dependent reactions capture solar energy and convert it into two portable forms the cell can spend elsewhere: ATP, generated as protons flow through ATP synthase down the gradient built by the chloroplast's electron transport chain, and NADPH, an electron-carrying molecule loaded with high-energy electrons pulled originally from water. Neither ATP nor NADPH is a stable long-term storage molecule, so a plant cannot simply keep making them and call it done. The Calvin cycle is the set of reactions, occurring in the stroma of the chloroplast, that spends this ATP and NADPH to build something the cell can actually store, transport, and burn later: sugar.

The cycle runs in three connected stages. In the first stage, carbon fixation, carbon dioxide from the air is attached to a five-carbon sugar already circulating in the stroma, ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate, forming an unstable six-carbon intermediate that immediately splits into two molecules of a three-carbon compound. In the second stage, reduction, each of those three-carbon molecules is first phosphorylated using ATP and then reduced using the high-energy electrons carried by NADPH, converting it into glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, commonly abbreviated G3P. This is the actual payoff step of the cycle, where energy from the light reactions gets locked into a stable carbon-hydrogen bond rather than staying in a phosphate bond or an electron carrier.

In the third stage, regeneration, most of the G3P produced is not exported from the cycle at all. Instead it is rearranged and further phosphorylated, spending additional ATP, to rebuild the five-carbon ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate that started the cycle, so the whole process can run again. Only a small fraction of the G3P produced actually leaves the cycle as net output, and it takes three full turns of the cycle, fixing three separate carbon dioxide molecules, to generate just one G3P molecule that the plant can use for something else, such as building glucose.

The bookkeeping matters because it shows how expensive sugar production really is. Fixing three carbon dioxide molecules into one net G3P requires nine ATP molecules and six NADPH molecules, all supplied by the light-dependent reactions. Scaling that up, producing a single six-carbon glucose molecule, which requires two G3P molecules combined, costs eighteen ATP and twelve NADPH, drawn from eighteen turns of ATP synthase's rotor and six passes of electrons all the way down the chloroplast's electron transport chain. Every sugar molecule a plant makes is, in a very real sense, a receipt showing exactly how much light energy was spent to make it.

This is also why the Calvin cycle, despite happening in the so-called dark reactions and not requiring light directly for any of its own chemical steps, cannot actually run in the dark for long. It depends entirely on a continuous supply of ATP and NADPH, and those run out quickly once the light reactions stop, since chloroplasts do not stockpile large reserves of either molecule. The Calvin cycle and the light-dependent reactions are best understood as one integrated system, not two separate processes, with the proton gradient and ATP synthase sitting at the hinge between them.
